purpose: What the batch route has to do to be acceptable — applied RETROSPECTIVELY. This is not a pre-registration and does not claim to be one. v2 inherited v1's sentence 'fixed before the recording exists', which was true of v1 and false of v2: v2 was written after the D1-7 recording by an author who already knew which verdict the new state would change. The sentence and the post-hoc note contradicted each other inside one file, and a file that contradicts itself about its own status is worse than one that overclaims plainly.

baseline.what: The same benchmark under the single-target contract, replayed offline from the phase7 recording. Regenerated rather than quoted: docs/baselines/melanoma_phase8_metrics.json publishes aggregates only, and a transition table needs rows.
baseline.label_accuracy: 66.7% (10 of 15) — reproduced, matching the published figure

reported_never_gated: label_accuracy — a system raises it by refusing less
claims_per_batch and cost — reported for v5 alone; no speedup is computed, because v5's single-target bucket holds arm identities and its batch bucket holds value claims, which are different tasks
excerpt coverage — a diagnostic about what was sent, not about the answer

allowed.correct -> refused: a capability loss. Reported, not forbidden: refusing is the safe direction, and this project has taken it deliberately before
allowed.refused -> correct: a capability gain, which is what batching is for
allowed.refused -> refused: unchanged, possibly for a different reason; the reason is reported
allowed.correct -> wrong_but_flagged: a capability loss with visibility intact. NOT a safety regression: the row was escalated, which is what the review path is for. It is counted and reported, and it is the state MA015 is actually in
allowed.refused -> wrong_but_flagged: same reasoning: escalated, so not released

forbidden.correct -> wrong_released: a row that was right now releases a wrong value with NO review flag. This is the safety regression the gate exists to catch
forbidden.refused -> wrong_released: a refusal replaced by an unreviewed wrong value is worse than the refusal
forbidden.wrong_but_flagged -> wrong_released: the value did not improve and the visibility was lost
forbidden.wrong_released -> wrong_released: not a pass. It was already a failure and remains one

outcome_rule: Four outcomes. NOT EVALUABLE when the gate's state space cannot express a transition that occurred — a fault of the gate, and recording it as a FAIL would attribute it to the system. FAIL on any forbidden transition, any unmet hard condition, or a breach of the capability floor. PASS when a floor is set and met. PASS (PROHIBITIONS ONLY) when no floor is set: every hard condition here is a prohibition, so a system that refused every row would satisfy all of them, and that verdict must not be readable as 'the route works'. None of these is evidence about a domain; the D6 cross-domain conclusion stays NOT ESTIMABLE regardless.
why_v2: v1 could not express what the D1-7 recording produced. It defines `wrong_released` as a wrong value released WITHOUT review, and MA015 was wrong AND review_required — a state v1 has no term for. The FAIL reported on the day came from an ad-hoc classifier written beside the result, which contradicted v1's own text; v1 itself never issued a verdict, and the correct record is NOT EVALUABLE. v1's bytes are unchanged. v2 adds the fourth state, an executable classifier (src/react_review/acceptance_transitions.py) so a verdict is reproducible rather than argued, and a capability floor — because every one of v1's hard conditions is a prohibition, and a system that refused every row satisfied all of them.

capability_floor.status: UNSET — deliberately, and this is not an oversight
capability_floor.why_unset: A draft of this file set the floor at 0.8. The D1-7 recording keeps 8 of the baseline's 10 correct rows, which is exactly 0.8 — the number was chosen after seeing the result and would have been a threshold fitted to pass it. That is the failure this whole governance apparatus exists to prevent, so the floor is left unset rather than published at a convenient value. The MECHANISM is implemented and tested, so setting it is a one-line decision rather than a redesign. Like the 0.70 recall bar in cross_domain, the value itself is blocked on a human saying what capability loss is tolerable; it is not an engineering choice.

what_this_gate_is.applies_to: the D1-7 recording and its reanalyses, as a diagnostic. Any result citing it must say so.
what_this_gate_is.what_a_pass_means: no prohibition was broken, on a gate written with the answer already visible. It is evidence that nothing forbidden happened; it is not evidence that the gate was hard to pass.
what_this_gate_is.for_a_real_pre_registration: a gate written before the next recording, with a capability floor set by someone who has not seen its result.

why_v3: v2 is not edited: it is published and a published file that changes retroactively describes runs it did not govern. v3 changes only what the gate SAYS ABOUT ITSELF — the hard conditions, the transitions, the baseline rows and the unset capability floor are byte-identical to v2, so no verdict moves because of this version.
retrospective_note: The D1-7 recording predates this file. Any result of applying v2 to it is a POST-HOC REANALYSIS and must be labelled so: the gate was changed after the run, in a direction its author knew would change the verdict. It is published because v1 could not judge the run at all, not because its verdict was inconvenient.
